Chapter 9:  Twenty Effects Of Food On The Human Body
Every Meal Is an Opportunity to Let Your Food Work For You Rather Than Against You

So far, we have explored the importance of a balanced diet, appropriate portion sizes  and proper meal timing. These are essential aspects of eating intelligently, but there is another important question we need to consider:                                What happens inside the body when we eat?                                                    Different foods interact with the body in different ways. Some nourish and strengthen, some protect and support, while others may provide specific benefits to various organs of the body. To deepen our understanding of intelligent eating, let us now examine twenty ways the foods we eat can affect and support our body
1. CALMING EFFECT

There are certain foods that can help calm your nerves when you are agitated or nervous and help you relax. These types of foods provide a steady release of glucose into the bloodstream, which can help stabilize mood and promote relaxation. They may help reduce anxiety and support overall mental health. Some contain precursors (that is, building blocks for the production of certain substances in the body) involved in the synthesis of substances that support relaxation and sleep. For example, tryptophan is an amino acid that the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin. Serotonin is a neurotransmitter that contributes to feelings of well-being and helps regulate mood.                                                                                                                                  Examples of food in this category are:                                                                                               (a) Whole grains such as oats, brown rice, quinoa, fonio.                                                              (b) Legumes such as beans, lentils, chickpeas.                                                                             (c) Poultry products  such as chicken, turkey, eggs.                                                                      (d) Fish such as salmon, mackerel and sardines, which are rich in omega-3 fatty acids.                                                                                     (e) Dairy products such as milk, yoghurt and cheese.                                                                    (f) Nuts and seeds such as almonds, walnuts, flaxseeds, chia seeds.                                          (g) Green vegetables such as spinach, lettuce and kale.                                                                 (h) Fruits such as blueberries, strawberries, raspberries, apples.                                         Others include: dark chocolate, green tea etc.
2. SEDATIVE EFFECT

These types of food can provide nutrients,  in some cases, naturally occurring compounds that may support the body's production of melatonin, the hormone that helps regulate sleep and the sleep-wake cycle. These foods may help promote relaxation and support better sleep quality, making it easier for some people to fall asleep.                                                                                                                                           Examples of foods in this category are:                                                                                             (a) Fruits such as bananas, cherries.                                                                                             (b) Nuts such as almonds, walnuts, cashews.                                                                           (c) Leafy green vegetables such as spinach, kale, lettuce, watercress.                                                                                                     (d) Whole grains such as oats, fonio,quinoa, brown rice.                                                         (e) Herbal teas such as chamomile tea, lavender tea, passionflower tea.                                                                                                                  (f) Warm milk, as mentioned earlier.
3. DIURETIC EFFECT

There are certain foods, herbs  and beverages that may promote increased urine production in the body. This diuretic effect can help the body eliminate excess fluid and support healthy fluid balance. Increased urination also supports the body's natural process of removing certain water-soluble waste products through the kidneys. Some diuretic foods are also naturally rich in water and nutrients, making them useful additions to a healthy diet. When included appropriately, they may support healthy kidney function, circulation  and fluid balance.                                                                            Examples of fruits, herbs and spices that may exert a diuretic effect include:                                                                                                            (a) Fruits such as cucumber, watermelon, lemon.                                                                        (b) Herbs: parsley, dandelion, nettle, horsetail, green tea,hibiscus, celery leaf etc.                                                                                                      (c ) Spice such as ginger, cumin,fennel,cinnamon, black pepper.
4. ASTRINGENT EFFECT

There are certain foods that have astringent properties. These foods can have a drying or contracting effect on body tissues and often leave a dry or puckering sensation in the mouth, particularly because of their tannin content. Astringent foods may help tone and tighten tissues, support healthy digestion and provide antioxidant benefits. Some also contain compounds with antimicrobial properties that may help the body defend itself against certain microorganisms.                                                                  Examples of foods with astringent properties include:                                                      (a)Fruits & Vegetables: pomegranate, green apples, cranberries, gooseberries, lemon, tamarind, cucumber, apricots,                                                                                                        (b) Seeds: sesame seeds,pumpkin seeds, sunflower etc.                                                                (c ) Black tea
5. ANTIOXIDANT EFFECT

Antioxidant-rich foods help protect our body cells from damage caused by free radicals. Free radicals can be generated naturally through normal processes in the body, as well as through exposure to external factors such as air pollution, cigarette smoke and radiation. When free radicals become excessive or the body is unable to balance them effectively, oxidative stress can occur. Over time, oxidative stress may contribute to cellular damage and has been associated with various health problems, including heart disease and some forms of cancer, as well as processes associated with ageing. Antioxidants found in many plant foods help the body neutralize free radicals and protect cells from oxidative damage. Making a variety of antioxidant-rich foods part of your diet is therefore an important way to support the body's natural defence and maintain overall health.

Examples of antioxidant-rich foods include:                                                                        1.Cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage, brussels sprouts.                                                                                              2. Berries such as blueberries, strawberries, raspberries, blackberries.                                                                                                    3. Nuts such as almonds, walnuts, pistachios.                                                                                   4. Green leafy vegetables.                                                                                                                5. Colourful fruits such as oranges, grapes, cherries  and pomegranates.                                                                                                     6. Legumes such as beans, lentils, chickpeas.                                                                                   7. Green tea                                                                                                                                           8. Spices such as turmeric, cinnamon, ginger, cloves.                                                                       9. Dark chocolate.
6. ANTI-SPASMODIC FOODS

There are foods that can prevent or relieve muscle spasms or cramps, they work by relaxing and calming the muscles, reducing their involuntary contractions or spasms.                                         Examples of foods that possess certain anti-spasmodic properties are:                                                                                                                (a) Fruits: banana, pineapple, avocado, oranges, papaya, watermelon, dates, apricots, and raisins.                                                                                                                                          (b) Magnesium-rich foods such as: dark leafy greens, nuts, seeds, legumes and whole grains.                                                                                                                                                   (c ) Fatty fish such as: salmon, mackerel,sardines.                                                                  (d)Spice: ginger,turmeric,cinnamon,fennel,cloves,black pepper etc.                                                                                  (e ) Herbal teas such as: passion flower,valerian root, lemon balm, chamomile,peppermint tea.
7. ANALGESIC FOODS

There are some foods that contain natural compounds that may help alleviate pain or discomfort. Many of these foods also have anti-inflammatory properties, which may help reduce inflammation and provide a degree of relief while supporting overall well-being. Because of these properties, such foods are sometimes described as having a “pain-relieving” effect. Including a variety of these foods in your diet can provide the body with anti-inflammatory nutrients and beneficial plant compounds that may support its natural response to inflammation and discomfort.                                           Examples of foods that may offer analgesic effects include:                                              (a)Spices & herbs :  ginger, turmeric, green tea.                                                                               (b) Fatty fish such as salmon, mackerel, sardines.                                                                        (c ) Extra virgin olive oil.                                                                                                                     (d) Dark leafy vegetables such as spinach, kale, swiss chard .                                            (e )Fruits: cherries, walnuts, almonds,pineapple,blueberries, strawberries, raspberries.                                                                         (f) Seeds: flaxseeds, chiaseeds,hemp seed, sunflower, sesame seeds.
8. ENERGY-BOOSTING EFFECT

There are certain foods that can help increase and sustain the body's energy levels because of their nutrient composition and their role in energy metabolism. They provide carbohydrates, protein, healthy fats, vitamins, minerals  and other nutrients that support the body's energy production and help reduce fatigue.                             Examples of energy-boosting foods include:                                                                                    (a) Whole grains and starchy foods such as oats and sweet potatoes, which provide carbohydrates for a steady supply of energy.                                                                                                                 (b) Fruits such as bananas, apples, berries and oranges, which provide natural sugars, fibre  and antioxidants for readily available energy.                                                                                                         (c) Protein-rich foods such as beans, lean meats, poultry, fish  and tofu, which provide amino acids that support energy metabolism, muscle function and recovery.                                                                     (d) Nuts and seeds such as almonds, walnuts, chia seeds and flaxseeds, which provide healthy fats, protein and fibre that help provide lasting energy.                                                                                            (e) Green leafy vegetables such as spinach and kale, which provide iron, magnesium, and other nutrients involved in energy production and may help reduce fatigue.                                                            (f) Dark chocolate.                                                                                                                             (g) Water, which is essential for normal body functions. Even mild dehydration can contribute to tiredness and fatigue.
9. ANTIMICROBIAL EFFECT

In this context, we are considering harmful microorganisms such as bacteria, viruses and fungi. These microorganisms are found everywhere; in the air, water, soil  and even within living organisms. Certain foods contain natural compounds with antimicrobial properties that may help the body defend itself against harmful microorganisms and support overall health.

These antimicrobial compounds may help inhibit the growth or activity of certain microorganisms, including bacteria, viruses and fungi.                                                                                                         Let’s look at this under these categories:                                                                                          (i ) ANTIFUNGAL EFFECT

Common fungal infections of the human body include athlete’s foot, ringworm, nail infections, vaginal yeast infections and some oral and oesophageal fungal infections. Certain foods and natural substances contain compounds with potential antifungal properties that may help inhibit the growth of certain fungi.                                           Examples include:                                                                                                                               (a) Coconut oil, apple cider vinegar, oregano oil, grapefruit seed extract,                                                                                                                   (b) Spice: ginger, garlic, oregano, thyme, cinnamon, cloves etc.
(ii) ANTIVIRAL EFFECT

Viral infections are caused by viruses and can include illnesses such as influenza (flu), the common cold, herpes, COVID-19  and measles, to mention a few. Certain foods contain compounds that have been associated with potential antiviral activity and may support the body's natural defences.                                                                                       Examples include:                                                                                                                               (a) Citrus fruits, berries, green tea, yoghurt,                                                                                   (b) Spice: garlic, ginger,turmeric etc.
(iii) ANTIBACTERIAL EFFECT

Certain foods contain natural compounds with antibacterial properties that may help inhibit the growth or activity of some bacteria and support the body's natural defence system.                                                                                                                                   Examples include:                                                                                                                                  (a) garlic,  ginger, turmeric, cinnamon,                                                                          (b)cranberries, green tea, honey,etc.
10. ANTI-PARASITIC EFFECT

There are certain foods and natural substances that contain compounds with potential anti-parasitic properties. When included as part of a wholesome diet, they may support the body's natural defences and digestive health. Some of these foods have traditionally been used to support the body when dealing with intestinal parasites and may help inhibit the growth or activity of certain parasites.                                                                            Examples of foods with anti-parasitic properties include:                                                          (a) Seeds: pumpkin seeds, papaya seeds, sunflower seeds,                                                         (b) garlic, onions, carrots.                                                                                                                   (b) fermented foods.
11. WEIGHT-MANAGEMENT EFFECT

The effect of food on body weight depends on several factors, including the type and quantity of food consumed, portion sizes, individual metabolism, physical activity  and overall dietary habits. Consistently consuming more energy than the body uses can contribute to weight gain, while consuming less energy than the body uses can contribute to weight loss. Certain foods can support healthy weight management by promoting feelings of fullness, providing essential nutrients, and helping to maintain stable energy levels.                                                                                                                    Examples include:                                                                                                                          (a) Whole grains: oat, quinoa,brown rice, maize,sorghum etc                                                                                                       (b) protein-rich foods such as lean meat, skinless poultry, fish, tofu, greek yoghurt, eggs  and legumes,                                                                                                                              (c ) Colourful fruits and vegetables,                                                                                           (d) Nuts and seeds: Sesame seed,almond,cashew nut, pumpkin seed etc                                                                                                              (e ) Herbs and spices such as cayenne pepper, ginger, turmeric and cinnamon, green tea and other wholesome foods.
12. ANTI-INFLAMMATORY EFFECT

Inflammation is the body's natural way of protecting itself from harmful stimuli and injury. It can cause symptoms such as pain, swelling, heat  and redness. Incorporating anti-inflammatory foods into your daily diet can help support the body's natural response to inflammation  and reduce the risk of some chronic diseases associated with persistent inflammation.                                                                                                       Examples are:                                                                                                                                       (a) Fatty fish such as salmon, sardines  and mackerel.                                                                 (b) Berries such as strawberries, blueberries, raspberries and blackberries.                                                                                                          (c )Dark leafy greens such as spinach, kale  and collard greens.                                                 (d) Others  are:turmeric, ginger, tomatoes, whole grains, nuts and seeds, etc.
13. ANTI-ANGIOGENIC EFFECT

Angiogenesis is the natural process by which the body forms new blood vessels. This is a normal and important process involved in growth, development  and tissue repair. However, some tumours can stimulate the formation of new blood vessels to obtain oxygen and nutrients which may support their continued growth. Certain foods contain natural compounds that have been studied for their potential anti-angiogenic properties. These compounds may influence some of the pathways involved in blood-vessel formation and may therefore have a supportive role in a healthy diet.                                                                                                            Including a variety of these foods in the diet may therefore provide beneficial plant compounds that support the body's natural protective processes.

Examples of foods and natural substances that have been studied for potential anti-angiogenic effects include:                                                                                                            (a) Seeds and oils such as  flaxseed and flaxseed oil                                                                       (b) Vegetables: kale, beetroot, artichokes, parsley, tomatoes, red onions and mushrooms                                                                                                                                           (c ) Spices and herbs such as  garlic, turmeric, nutmeg, lavender, ginseng, cinnamon and liquorice.                                                                                                                                  (d) Beverages and other foods like green tea, herbal tea, tigernut drink, olive oil  and grapes.                                                                                                                                              (e) Seafood such as tuna, sea cucumbers and dark chocolate.

PLEASE NOTE                                                                                                                             Shark cartilage and shark liver oil have been discussed in some natural-health literature for their potential anti-angiogenic properties. They have been proposed as substances that may influence the formation of new blood vessels; however, current evidence is not sufficient to establish this claim.Their potential role as supportive measures alongside appropriate treatment remains an area that warrants further research.
14. ANTI-METASTATIC EFFECT

Cancerous cells can metastasise, meaning they can spread from their primary location to other parts of the body, forming secondary growths. There are certain foods that contain natural compounds that have been studied for their potential anti-metastatic properties. These foods may help support the body's natural protective mechanisms and may influence some of the processes involved in the spread of cancerous cells.

The aim is to support the body in maintaining a healthy internal environment and, potentially, help limit processes associated with cancer cell invasion and spread.                                                           Examples of foods in this category are:                                                                                          (a) Fruits such as berries, citrus fruits, avocado,walnuts                                                                 (b) Cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, cauliflower, brussels sprouts and kale, tomatoes, leafy greens.                                                                                                                                                     (c )Fatty fish such as mackerel and salmon.                                                                          (d)Others are whole grains, legumes, healthy fats, flaxseeds, chia seeds, almonds,green tea etc.

Please note                                                                                                                                       Many of the foods mentioned above contain compounds that are being investigated for their potential effects on cancer-cell invasion, migration, and other processes associated with metastasis. While this area of nutrition and cancer research is promising, the extent to which dietary intake can directly prevent or stop metastasis requires further scientific investigation.
15. IMMUNE-MODULATING EFFECT

The immune system needs to maintain a healthy balance. When it is too weak, the body may have difficulty defending itself against infections and other challenges. When it becomes overactive or improperly regulated, it may contribute to inflammatory and autoimmune conditions. Certain foods contain nutrients and natural compounds that may help modulate or regulate immune function. In other words, they may support the immune system when it needs strengthening while also helping to maintain a balanced immune response.                                                                    Examples of such foods are:                                                                                                             (a) citrus fruits,like oranges, grapefruits, lemons, and limes.                                                     (b) berries such as raspberries, strawberries and blueberries.                                        (c )Others are: garlic, ginger, yoghurt, green leafy vegetables such as spinach, kale and broccoli, turmeric, mushrooms, almonds, green tea, etc.

Please note:                                                                                                                                        The immune-modulating properties of many foods and their bioactive compounds are being actively studied. Their effects may vary depending on the individual, the food consumed and the person's health status. This makes the relationship between nutrition and immune regulation an important area for continued research.
16. HORMONE-BALANCING EFFECT

Hormonal imbalance can affect many functions in the body and may contribute to a variety of health concerns, particularly in women. Certain foods provide nutrients and natural compounds that may help support healthy hormone production, metabolism and regulation.                                                                                                                       Examples include:                                                                                                                          (a) Cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, cabbage and brussels sprouts.                                                                                                        (b) Nuts and seeds: flaxseeds, chiaseeds, pumpkin seeds, sunflower, almond.                                                                                                          (c ) Fermented foods such as yoghurt, sauerkraut and kefir,                                                   (d) soy products such as tofu and tempeh,                                                                                  (e ) Others are : berries,avocado, salmon, dark chocolate,  etc.
17. DETOXIFYING EFFECT

There are certain foods that contain nutrients and natural compounds that can support the body's natural detoxification processes. Many are also rich in fibre and water, which can support regular bowel movements and the healthy elimination of waste from the digestive system.                                                                                         Examples include:                                                                                                                       (a)Spices:  turmeric, garlic, ginger,                                                                                          (b)Fruits & Vegetables:  artichokes, beetroot,grapefruit, collard greens, lemon, dandelion, broccoli, watercress, seaweed.                                                                                 (c ) Others are: Water, lemongrass, basil.
18. ALKALIZING EFFECT

There are certain foods that can help support the body's acid-base balance. Many of these foods are rich in minerals and other nutrients, including potassium, magnesium and calcium. Although foods can influence the body's acid load, the body carefully regulates blood pH through the lungs and kidneys.                                                            Examples include:                                                                                                                                 (a) Fruits: Cucumber, avocado,watermelon , lemons etc                                                                                                                (b) Others are:  leafy green vegetables, broccoli, almonds, celery  etc.

19. Oxygenating Effect :                                                                                                       There are certain foods that can support oxygenation in the body by providing nutrients necessary for optimal respiratory function and healthy blood circulation. These foods may help support the body’s ability to transport and use oxygen effectively.                                                                                                                                        Examples of foods that could help to support oxygenation are foods rich in omega-3 fatty acids, such as:                                                                                                                             (a)  flax seed, chia seeds, hemp seeds,                                                                                         (b) Fatty fish such as salmon, mackerel, sardines,trout and tuna, algal oil,                                                                                                       (c )soybeans and soy products,                                                                                                        (d) beetroot, citrus fruits, watermelon,walnuts,                                                                           (e ) Others are:  leafy green vegetables,, dark chocolate, turmeric, ginger,garlic, legumes etc
Anti-Neoplastic Effect.

Anti-neoplastic foods contain nutrients and natural compounds that have been studied for their potential anti-cancer properties. These foods may support the body’s natural protective mechanisms and contribute to a healthy dietary pattern.             Examples are:                                                                                                                          cruciferous vegetables such as  broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage, brussels sprouts, kale, collard greens,  watercress, radishes and mustard greens, berries, garlic,  soursop etc

When you understand the work food can do in your body, you begin to make food choices with greater wisdom and intention. Food is more than something placed on a plate. The choices we make every day can become an expression of how intentionally we care for the body God has entrusted to us.
Eat intelligently. Let your food work for you. Nourish your body wisely.
Reflect & Journal
Take a moment to reflect on what you have discovered about the many ways food can interact with and support your body.
Which of the effects of food discussed in this chapter was most surprising or meaningful to me, and why?
Do I now look at food differently as simply something to satisfy hunger, or as something that can also nourish, protect and support my body?
3. Which foods in my regular diet could I begin choosing more intentionally because of the benefits they may offer?
4.Are there foods I regularly consume that may be working against the health I desire?
Today's Action
Before eating, look at your plate and ask yourself:
What is this food going to do for my body?
Choose a variety of wholesome foods and eat slowly and mindfully. As you eat, pay attention to the colour, aroma, taste, texture, and how satisfied you feel.

Scriptural Reference

‘’Healing begins long before you enter a hospital; it begins with what you put on your plate each day’’
Chapter 10:  Ten Commandments of Healthy Living

As I conclude this insightful journey into what intelligent eating is all about, I would like to include a short note from one of my itinerant health presentations, where I spoke on the topic:  “10 Commandments of Healthy Living.”

Just as God gave the Israelites the Ten Commandments through Moses as guiding principles for righteous living,  I have, based on my knowledge and experience in naturopathy and healthy living, summed up some of the fundamental principles of healthy living into ten simple instructions.

I call them the “10 Commandments of Healthy Living” because they are practical principles that I believe we should intentionally and consistently practise to help prevent disease, support the body's natural healing processes and promote better health, particularly when we are experiencing ill-health or managing a health condition.

The word “commandments” is used here to emphasise the importance of making these healthy practices a consistent and intentional part of our daily lives. These ten principles are drawn from my experience in naturopathy and my commitment to promoting healthy living principles that I have personally practised and taught others over the years.
My desire is to encourage you to care wisely for the body God has given to you and to make healthy living a consistent part of your daily life.
1. Start Your Day with Water

After several hours of sleep, your body has gone without water, so beginning your morning with water is a simple way to rehydrate and support normal body functions. Warm or room-temperature water can be soothing and may also help get the digestive system moving and support a regular bowel movement, especially when you are adequately hydrated throughout the day.

As you go through your early morning routine; praying, doing a little exercise, cleaning, or simply preparing for the day,you can gradually drink about 50–70 cl of warm or room-temperature water. After drinking the water, allow about one hour before having breakfast
Starting the day this way can help you feel refreshed, hydrated and ready for the day ahead.
2. Drink Enough Water Throughout the Day

Scientific research shows that about 60% of the human body is water. This alone tells us how important water is to the proper functioning of our organs and body systems. Every organ and body system depends on adequate hydration to function properly. Water helps transport nutrients, regulate body temperature, support digestion and remove waste products from the body. Staying well hydrated is one of the simplest ways to care for the body God has given us.

While your daily water needs vary according to factors such as your activity level, climate, diet and individual needs, make water your primary drink. Do not wait until you feel very thirsty before drinking; develop the habit of taking water regularly throughout the day.

When you are thirsty, choose water rather than reaching for a carbonated or sugary drink. Although such drinks contain water and can contribute to your fluid intake, they are not the best substitute for plain water. Many contain added sugars, artificial sweeteners, acids, caffeine, or other additives that can make them less desirable as your everyday source of hydration. Regularly choosing these drinks instead of water may also increase your intake of unnecessary sugar and calories. When your body is asking for water, give it water!
3. Eat Fruits Every Day

Fruits are one of the simplest and most enjoyable ways to nourish the body naturally. They provide vitamins, minerals, fibre, antioxidants and other beneficial plant nutrients that support the body's normal functions and contribute to overall health.

From my perspective in naturopathy and healthy living, I encourage making fruits a regular part of your diet rather than seeing them as something to eat only occasionally. Nature has given us an amazing variety of fruits, each with its own colour, flavour and nutrients.

Fruits can also be a healthier way to satisfy the desire for something sweet. Choosing a naturally sweet fruit instead of sweets, pastries, or sugary snacks may help you reduce your intake of added sugars and, for some people, curb the desire for highly processed sweet foods.

You do not have to eat the same fruit every day. Enjoy variety. Eat what is available and in season. Enjoy fruits that are naturally grown in your environment. You can eat them whole, add them to meals, enjoy them as a snack, fruit juice or nutritious smoothies when appropriate.
Fruits are also a wonderful reminder of God's provision. From the beginning, God provided fruit-bearing trees and plants as food for humanity.
4. Get Enough Quality Sleep

Sleep is not a luxury or a sign of laziness; it is an essential part of caring for the body God has entrusted to us. Just as the body needs nourishing food and adequate water, it also needs sufficient rest to function at its best.

While we sleep, the body is not simply “switched off.” It enters a period of restoration and repair. During quality sleep, the body carries out important processes that support the immune system, brain function, tissue repair and overall recovery. This is why consistently depriving yourself of sleep can eventually affect your health.

As a healthy-living enthusiast, I encourage people not only to get enough sleep but also to develop a healthy sleep rhythm. Our bodies have an internal biological clock, known as the circadian rhythm, which helps regulate our natural sleep-wake cycle and responds to the daily pattern of light and darkness. Going to bed at a reasonably early and consistent time allows us to work with, rather than against, this natural rhythm.

This is also one reason I encourage you to finish your evening meal about 2–3 hours before bedtime whenever possible. Going to bed immediately after a heavy meal means your digestive system is still actively processing food while your body is preparing for nighttime rest. Allowing some time after dinner gives your body an opportunity to settle before sleep and may help you sleep more comfortably.

The late-night hours should therefore be treated as a time for rest, restoration and the body's normal maintenance processes, rather than a time for heavy meals, unnecessary snacking or staying awake unnecessarily.
Although sleep requirements vary with age and individual needs, most adults need about 7–9 hours of quality sleep each night. Children and teenagers generally require more.
Eat early. Rest well. Give your body time to restore.
5. Enjoy Daily Sunlight

Sunlight is one of God's natural provisions, given to support our overall well-being. Early morning sunlight contains ultraviolet B (UVB) rays, which help the skin produce vitamin D, an important nutrient for healthy bones, muscles and normal immune function.Spending some time outdoors each day can be beneficial to our emotional well-being and may help improve mood especially for people experiencing low mood or a state of depression.

As a healthy-living enthusiast, I encourage making appropriate sunlight a regular part of your daily routine. You do not need to spend long hours in the sun. The goal is sensible, regular exposure, not prolonged exposure that leaves the skin burning or damaged.

For those living in Nigeria, as well as other tropical and sub-Saharan regions, sunlight can become intense relatively early in the day. Early morning is therefore a comfortable time for many people to enjoy outdoor light, although the appropriate duration varies with skin type, location, season and the strength of the sun.

You can combine your sunlight time with other healthy habits: take a morning prayer walk, exercise, read or simply sit quietly and enjoy the free gift of sunlight God has provided. Avoid looking directly at the sun and when the sun becomes intense, seek shade or use appropriate protection such as clothing, a hat or sunscreen.
Enjoy God's sunlight wisely; not too little, not too much, but in a way that supports your health while protecting your skin.
6. Practise Intermittent Fasting Weekly

Intermittent fasting is the intentional practice of creating a period when you do not eat, followed by a defined period in which you eat. One of the most commonly studied approaches is the 16:8 method. Out of the 24 hours in a day, 16 hours will be allotted  for fasting followed by an 8-hour eating window. During the fasting period, water and other calorie-free drinks may be taken.

Fasting gives the body a break from continuous eating and allows you to become more intentional about when, why and how much you eat. It can help reduce unnecessary snacking and for some people, support healthy weight management and blood-sugar regulation. Research has also found improvements in some measures of insulin resistance and glucose regulation among certain people following time-restricted eating.
How Does the 16:8 Method Work?
You choose an 8 hour eating window and allow the remaining 16 hours for fasting.
For example:
12:00 noon – 8:00 p.m.: Eating window8:00 p.m. – 12:00 noon the following day: Fasting window
During the fasting period, drink water regularly. Avoid sugary drinks and other calorie-containing beverages if you want to maintain the fasting period.
You can adjust the timing of your 8 hour eating window to suit your lifestyle. What matters is developing a consistent pattern rather than fasting randomly.
What Happens During the Fast?

When you stop eating, your body continues to use the energy already available to it. As the fasting period progresses, the body can increasingly draw on stored energy, including stored fat, although the extent varies from person to person. Intermittent fasting may also naturally reduce overall food intake because there is less time available for eating.

This is one reason I encourage fasting as part of a broader healthy-living lifestyle, not as a punishment for eating, but as a way of developing discipline, intentionality and a healthier relationship with food.
What Should You Eat During the 8 Hour Window?

Fasting does not give us permission to spend the eating window eating whatever we want. The quality of your food still matters. Make your meals nourishing and balanced, with plenty of vegetables, whole fruits, legumes, whole grains, healthy fats and appropriate protein sources. Avoid using the eating window as an opportunity to overeat highly processed foods, sugary drinks or excessive snacks.

If you have been fasting for several hours, break your fast gently rather than rushing into a very large meal. A meal containing wholesome, minimally processed foods is a better way to nourish the body.
Any Health Benefit?

For some adults, particularly those with overweight, obesity, prediabetes or type 2 diabetes, time-restricted eating may support weight management and improve aspects of blood-glucose regulation. However, fasting should be viewed as one possible lifestyle adjustment that, when practised appropriately and consistently, can become part of a healthy-living routine. It should not be regarded as a cure for disease.

If you have diabetes, especially if you use insulin or certain blood-sugar lowering medicines, do not begin intermittent fasting without appropriate medical guidance. Fasting can cause dangerously low or high blood sugar in some circumstances and medication timing or dosage may need to be adjusted.
Fasting is not only about food. Throughout Scripture, fasting is associated with prayer, humility, self-control and seeking God.
“When you fast...”  Matthew 6:16–18
Use your fasting period as an opportunity to pray, reflect, exercise self-discipline and become more conscious of your physical and spiritual needs.
Fast with purpose. Eat with wisdom. Nourish your body intentionally.
7. Exercise Regularly

Our bodies were made to move. Exercise is not only about losing weight or changing how you look; it is one of the simple ways we care for the body God has entrusted to us. When we move regularly, we strengthen our muscles and bones, support heart health, improve circulation and promote emotional well-being.

As a healthy-living enthusiast, I encourage you not to see exercise as something you do only when you want to lose weight or when you have time for the gym. Movement should become part of your everyday life. You do not need expensive equipment or a gym membership to stay active. A brisk walk, jogging, dancing, cycling, swimming, skipping, stretching, gardening, household chores, or simple exercises at home can all keep your body moving.

The important thing is to choose activities you enjoy and can do consistently. You may prefer a morning walk, a few stretches after waking up, dancing to your favourite music, or an evening walk after work. There is no need to make exercise complicated. What matters is making movement a regular part of your lifestyle.

Regular physical activity can help strengthen the heart, improve circulation, maintain healthy muscles and bones, support healthy weight management, improve blood-sugar regulation, increase stamina, reduce stress, improve mood  and promote better sleep. It can also help you maintain mobility and independence as you grow older.

If you have been inactive for some time, do not feel pressured to start with intense exercise. Start where you are and build gradually. Even short periods of movement throughout the day are better than sitting for long periods without activity. Listen to your body, stay hydrated and give yourself enough time to recover.

Remember, exercise should strengthen and support your body, not become a punishment. You do not have to exhaust yourself to benefit from movement. Find something you enjoy, make it part of your routine, and keep going.
Move your body. Enjoy the gift of movement.
8. Eat More Natural Foods and Less Processed Food

Natural foods are foods that come from nature, whether from the land or water, and have undergone little or no processing before we eat them. They include fresh fruits, vegetables, legumes, whole grains, nuts, seeds, seafood and other foods that remain close to their original form.

Processed foods, on the other hand, are foods that originally come from natural sources but have undergone some form of preparation or alteration before they are eaten. This may involve cooking, drying, milling, freezing, canning, fermentation, or adding ingredients to improve their taste, texture, appearance, or shelf life.

Although food processing can have useful purposes, such as preserving food, improving safety and extending its shelf life.      The more a food is altered, the further it may move from its original form. Some processing methods can reduce certain nutrients, while added ingredients such as excess salt, sugar, unhealthy fats, colours, flavours and preservatives may make the food less desirable as an everyday choice.

This is why I encourage making natural and minimally processed foods the mainstay of your diet whenever possible. Foods in their natural or simple form generally provide the body with a combination of nutrients, fibre and other beneficial substances without the need for unnecessary additives.

For example, fresh carrot can be eaten raw when appropriate or gently cooked, allowing you to enjoy its natural nutrients and fibre. Compare this with some canned vegetables, which may contain added salt or other ingredients used during processing and preservation.                                                                                                                                   The same applies to fruits:                                                                                                             A fresh orange provides fibre, vitamins, minerals and other beneficial plant substances in its natural form. This is quite different from a packaged fruit drink that may contain added sugar, flavourings, preservatives and only a small fraction of the nutritional value of the whole fruit.

Your body is wonderfully equipped to digest and use nutrients from food. Why complicate what nature has already provided? Whenever possible, choose foods that are close to their original form, prepare them simply and enjoy the nourishment they provide.

This does not mean that every processed food is bad or that you must completely eliminate all foods that have been processed. Processing can sometimes make food safer, more convenient, or easier to store. The concern is with relying heavily on highly processed foods that have been altered considerably and often contain excess sugar, salt, unhealthy fats and additives while providing relatively little nutritional value.

A simple way to make better choices is to let natural or minimally processed foods form the foundation of your meals. Choose fresh fruits and vegetables, beans and other legumes, whole grains, nuts, seeds and other wholesome foods more often. When possible, prepare your meals yourself so you have greater control over what goes into them.

Learn to read food labels too. The longer and more complicated the ingredient list,  the more carefully you should consider what you are buying. Do not be deceived by attractive packaging or health claims on the label of a product. Turn the package around, look at the ingredients and nutritional information.

Another helpful habit is to gradually reduce your dependence on sugary drinks, packaged snacks, instant meals, refined foods, processed meats and other highly processed foods. You do not have to change everything overnight. Small, consistent changes can make a significant difference over time.

Think of it this way: eat foods that look more like the foods God created and less like the products manufactured in a factory.                                                                                                 The goal is not perfection; it is to make wholesome choices more often.
Choose real food more often. Read your labels. Nourish your body wisely.
9. Rest and Avoid Excessive Stress

Life can be demanding. There will always be responsibilities and challenges beyond our control. However, living under constant stress and worry can take a toll on both the mind and the body. This is why rest, relaxation and learning how to manage stress are important parts of healthy living.

Rest is more than simply sleeping at night. It also means giving your mind and body regular opportunities to slow down, recover and recharge. Make time to pause from work and daily responsibilities. Take a walk, spend time in nature, pray, listen to music, go on vacation, enjoy meaningful conversations, or simply sit quietly without feeling guilty about doing nothing.

Pay attention to the things that continually leave you feeling overwhelmed. Sometimes healthy living requires us to slow down, set boundaries, say no when necessary and stop carrying responsibilities that are beyond our control. You cannot always change what is happening around you, but you can learn healthier ways to respond to it.

Stress itself is not always harmful. Short periods of stress are a normal part of life. The concern is persistent or excessive stress without adequate recovery. When stress becomes constant, it can affect sleep, mood, appetite, concentration and other aspects of well-being.

As part of a healthy lifestyle, make rest intentional. Do not wait until your body breaks down before you give it permission to rest. Build moments of rest into your daily routine and allow yourself time away from work and unnecessary demands.
Most importantly, learn to take your worries to God. Prayer, gratitude, faith  and trusting God can help bring perspective and peace when life feels overwhelming.
Rest is not laziness, and taking a break does not mean you are unproductive. Sometimes, resting is exactly what the body and mind need to continue well.
Slow down. Breathe. Rest. Trust God. Live well.
10. Maintain a Healthy Social Life

We were not created to live in isolation. Healthy relationships are an important part of a healthy life. Family, friends, neighbours, colleagues and other meaningful relationships can provide love, encouragement, companionship, accountability and emotional support.

Having people you can talk to, laugh with, pray with, share your experiences with and turn to when life becomes difficult can make a real difference to your overall well-being. Positive social connections can help reduce feelings of loneliness, lift your mood and give you a sense of belonging and purpose.

However, maintaining a healthy social life is not about having a large number of friends or being constantly surrounded by people. It is about having meaningful and healthy relationships. Choose relationships that encourage growth, mutual respect, honesty, kindness and peace. At the same time, learn to recognise relationships that consistently drain you, encourage unhealthy habits, or rob you of your peace. Always avoid toxic relationship.

Be intentional about staying connected. Call someone you care about, visit a loved one, share a meal, take a walk together, join a meaningful group, or simply spend quality time with the people who matter to you. Sometimes, a simple conversation or a listening ear is all someone needs.

Healthy relationships also require us to play our own part. Be the kind of friend, family member, neighbour, or colleague you would want to have. Listen when others need to talk, offer encouragement, forgive where possible, apologise when you are wrong and celebrate the successes of others.
Your social well-being is connected to your emotional and mental well-being. A healthy life is not only about what you eat or how much you exercise; it is also about the people you share life with.
Connect meaningfully. Love generously. Grow together. Live well.

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Transforming Your Kitchen into a Natural Pharmacy
paragraphs: “The greatest medicine of all is teaching people how not to need it.” Hippocrates
Your kitchen may be one of the most powerful places in your home when it comes to your health.
Every day, you make choices about what enters your body. Some foods nourish, protect and strengthen the body, while others may simply satisfy hunger without providing much nutritional value.
This is why your kitchen deserves intentional attention.
What if your kitchen could become a place that supports healing, nourishment and prevention?

The goal is not to turn your kitchen into a literal pharmacy or to suggest that food replaces necessary medical treatment. Rather, it is to make your kitchen a place where real, nourishing foods and natural ingredients are readily available and where healthy choices become the easier choices.
What Should a Natural Kitchen Look Like?
A natural kitchen is not necessarily an expensive kitchen. It is a kitchen where whole and minimally processed foods have a prominent place.
A Simple Kitchen Transformation
You do not have to empty your kitchen overnight.  Start gradually.
Replace.Replace sugary drinks with water more often.
Reduce.Reduce your dependence on highly processed foods.
Add.Add more fruits, vegetables, legumes, whole grains, herbs and spices.
Prepare.Prepare more of your meals from recognizable ingredients.
Invest.Purchase kitchen equipment that makes healthy preparation easier.
Organize.Place nourishing foods where they are easy to see and reach.
Your kitchen does not have to be perfect.
It simply needs to become more intentional.
Reflect & Journal
Today's Action

Give your kitchen a health makeover.                                                                                      Open your refrigerator, freezer, cupboards and pantry.                                                     Sort what you find into four simple categories:                                                                         1. KEEP:Nourishing foods you want to eat regularly.                                                                                  2. REDUCE:Foods you want to consume less frequently.                                                                                  3. REPLACE:Less nourishing choices for which you can find better alternatives.                                       4. ADD:Whole foods, fruits, vegetables, herbs, spices and other nourishing ingredients you want to introduce.
Then choose one kitchen appliance or tool that would make healthy food preparation easier for you.
Scriptural Reference
“Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.”    1 Corinthians 10:31
Eat Intelligently Tip
Do not just stock your kitchen, design it.
A kitchen filled with nourishing ingredients, useful tools and ready-to-eat healthy options can make intelligent eating easier every day.
Your kitchen should help you practise what you have learned in this journal.
Conclusion:  Your Journey to Lifelong Healthy Living
Your journey through Eat Intelligently may be coming to an end, but your journey to healthy living is just beginning.

You have learned that food is more than something that fills the stomach.  It can nourish, protect, strengthen and support the body. You have explored the importance of eating wholesome foods, making wise choices, understanding portions, choosing natural ingredients and creating habits that support your well-being.
Healthy living is not about perfection; it is about consistent, intentional choices. Every meal, every habit and every day gives you another opportunity to care for your body.
My Personal Commitment

I commit to making my health a daily priority.                                                                                  I will:                                                                                                                                              choose nourishing, wholesome foods more often.                                                                 drink enough water and reduce unnecessary sugary drinks.                                             include more fruits and vegetables in my meals.                                                                  practice mindful eating and pay attention to portion sizes.                                                  make healthier choices when shopping and preparing food.                                                    stay physically active and make time for adequate rest.                                                          avoid the mindset of perfection and simply get back on track when I make a poor choice.                                                                                                                                          continue learning and improving my lifestyle one step at a time.
I will not wait for a health challenge before I begin to take care of myself. I will start where I am, use what I have, and make better choices each day.
Remember, your health is a journey, not a destination.                                                             Take it one meal, one choice and one day at a time.
Eat intelligently. Live intentionally. Nourish your body. Protect your future.
Here’s to a healthier, wiser and more intentional you.
